p: Tuesday, August 3, Maria came up the stairs at 6:58 with two coffees and the list. The light in the analysts' room was on. It had probably never gone off.

Kiran was at his desk in yesterday's shirt. The thirty-one failed scripts were on the whiteboard behind him in three colors, sorted by system, then by severity, then by which ones shared a cause. It was beautiful work. It had taken most of the night.
I went home, he said before she could ask. At one. Then I came back at five, because I knew where to start. He said it like good news.

She set a coffee in front of him. Monday's page of her legal pad still said KIRAN at the top, underlined twice, the way it had since April. She'd told Kiran to go home so many times it had stopped sounding like anything. Show me the first one, she said.

He put it on the big screen. Script one, the one she'd written herself in April and Walt had voted to the top of the list. A Rawlins test patient, seventy-four years old, twenty-three active medications, transferred to Greeley. On Corvane's admission screen, twenty medications sat in a neat column. No banner. No count. Nothing to say the list had ever been longer.

Maria looked at it the way she used to look at a monitor at four in the morning, waiting for a number to change. It didn't. Three medications had left Rawlins and never arrived, and the screen was perfectly calm about it.
Kiran was already reaching for the keyboard. I think I know where. Give me an hour in the build and I can... No, Maria said, and surprised them both. Get Marcus. And eat something.
Ochoa's Legal Pad: proving it works.

The Sunday after the first failed cycle, Ochoa took the back booth at the Greeley diner and wrote the kinds of testing down the legal pad, smallest to biggest. Every one of these answers a different question, he said. Skip one and you don't skip the question. You just hear it later, from a patient.

Unit testing checks one piece by itself: an order set, a mapping, one interface's translation. The builder usually runs it. System testing checks a whole application against its design, every screen and rule in Corvane working together. Integrated testing runs real workflows across systems and interfaces, from registration through orders, pharmacy, the eMAR, results, and billing, with test patients. In a migration most defects live between systems, so this is where they turn up.

Regression testing reruns tests that already passed, after any change, to prove the fix didn't break something else. Volume or load testing runs the expected peak, all of Monday morning at once, to find where the system slows. Stress testing pushes past that peak to find where it breaks. User acceptance testing, UAT, is the last gate. The people who'll use the system run their own scenarios and decide whether it's ready, and its owners sign.

How the exam asks it. Expect a scenario that describes a test and asks its type. One piece alone is unit, one whole application is system, systems together are integrated, a rerun after a change is regression, the expected peak is volume or load, past the peak until it breaks is stress, and users deciding readiness is acceptance.

Each test script lists steps, test data, and an expected result. When the actual result differs, it's a defect, logged with the steps to reproduce it and a severity: one stops care or risks harm, four is cosmetic. Two measures track each build. Pass rate is scripts passed divided by scripts executed. Defect density is defects divided by the size of what you tested, here per test script. Other teams count per function point or per thousand lines of code. Say which, and use the same one every build.

Before testing starts, write entry and exit criteria, like 95 percent passed and no open severity one or two defects. Then trace every requirement and every acceptance test in the contract to a script that proves it. That traceability matrix is how you validate a build against the contract and the design specs, and it shows any requirement nobody tested. Test the edges, too. A limit of twenty needs a test at nineteen, twenty, twenty-one, and well past it.

How the exam asks it. Expect to compute a pass rate or defect density from a table. A deliverable is accepted when it passes the test written from the contract and design, not when the vendor says it's done.

Testing needs controls of its own. Keep separate environments for build, test, and production. Give every build a version number, so a passing result points to exactly what passed. Move nothing between environments without a change ticket, and move by ticket, not by date. Separate the duties: whoever builds a change doesn't test it, approve it, or move it alone.

Test security as well. Sign in with test accounts that carry the same roles real users will have, check the audit logs, and scan for vulnerabilities before go-live. Use test patients or masked data. Real patient data in a test system needs every protection it has in production.
How the exam asks it. When one person can build, test, and promote a change, the missing control is segregation of duties. When nobody can say which build passed, it's version control.

Technical change management decides what changes in a live system, and when. A request for change says what will change and why, what it touches, the test evidence, and a back-out plan. The change advisory board weighs the risk, then approves it, schedules it, or sends it back. Standard changes are routine and preapproved. Emergency changes get fast approval from an emergency CAB or a named authority, then a full review after. Before go-live, most teams freeze everything but fixes.
Watch the shared parts, Ochoa said. When eleven hospitals run on one system, a change built for three of them reaches all eleven, unless somebody proves it doesn't.
How the exam asks it. Expect the board to want impact analysis, test evidence, a back-out plan, and a schedule. "No clinical impact" is a claim to check, not a reason to approve.

A project holds scope, schedule, budget, and quality together, and moving one moves another. Quality is the one people cut without saying so, by cutting tests. When the date is at risk, make the trade in the open: defer scope through change control, add people or money, or move the date, and let the sponsor decide with the facts.

Every project draws on the same people, so run them as a portfolio. List every project with its people, rank them against strategy and risk, and defer what can wait, with dates. Then look at the people themselves. Staff competency means a defined skill, practice, and a sign-off from someone who watched, so no skill lives in one person.
How the exam asks it. When the date is threatened, pick the answer that makes the tradeoff visible and keeps the testing. When one person holds a skill, train and verify a second.

Help desk tickets are monitoring data. Group them by time, place, and the words people use, and line them up against recent changes. Twenty tickets that start an hour after a change are one problem, not twenty incidents. Restore service first, then find the root cause.

Test the rest the same way. Under volume, check the network: clinical traffic gets priority, and scheduled jobs shouldn't all fire in the same minute. In UAT, watch whether each screen puts what the clinician needs where the decision happens. And govern every alert that goes live at a new site, the same as at home.
Ochoa tore the page off. A test that passes tells you less than one that fails, he said. Love the ones that fail. They're the cheap ones.

How the exam asks it. For a spike in tickets, correlate before you fix. For a network that slows under load, prioritize clinical traffic and spread scheduled jobs before you buy bandwidth. Alerts at a new site go through the same governance as the rest.
Marcus came up from the basement at 7:20 with one of his junior analysts and a printout he'd marked in red. He didn't sit. Each half works, he said. That's the problem.

It took him four minutes. Tributary turned MedaLink's transfer summary into FHIR and handed the medication list to Corvane twenty at a time, in pages, with a link to the next page at the bottom. Corvane read page one and never asked for page two. The banner Maria had written into script one compared the count to what had arrived, and it took the count from page one, which said twenty. Tributary tested with a patient on nine meds, Marcus said. Corvane tested the banner with a message somebody typed. Both passed. Nobody tested the handoff with more than twenty.

In her head Maria was back at Irene's kitchen table in May, the two of them saying it to each other. There was a page two. She put her hand flat on the desk and left it there until the room was this year again. Kiran was watching her. So was Marcus. He'd known her long enough to see it, and not long enough to ask.
A. Log it as severity one, trace the whole handoff, and test the limits.
B. Log a defect with each vendor, and retest when each says it's fixed.
C. Call it a known issue, and have nurses call the sender for long lists.
D. Have Kiran set Corvane to read every page tonight, then rerun script one.

Maria logs it herself, severity one, with the steps, the test patient, twenty-three expected, twenty actual. Marcus owns the path end to end, with both vendors on one call by nine. Corvane will follow every next link, and the banner will take its count from MedaLink's own total. Marcus's analyst writes new scripts at the edges: zero, nineteen, twenty, twenty-one, and forty. She finds two more feeds that read in pages. Good, Marcus says, and nothing else.

That's the move. Integrated testing finds defects that unit tests can't, because they live between systems. Log each one with steps, expected and actual results, and a severity. Give the whole path one owner. Then test the boundaries, where limits like twenty hide.

That night she called Irene. They talked most Sundays now, but this couldn't wait for Sunday. Maria told it plainly. A test patient, twenty-three medications, twenty on the screen. Irene was quiet a moment. Where'd you go, when you saw it? Your kitchen. Then the unit. Me too, just now. Then, drier: So you found page two in a test. With nobody in the bed. That's a mock code, Santos.

Friday, August 6, Corvane's project director sent the plan for the rest of testing. Two more integrated cycles, on August 23 and September 13. Then go-live. Beside stress testing he'd written two words: not needed. Eight hospitals already ran on the same Corvane system every day. User acceptance would be done by Corvane's trainers, who knew the scripts best.
Gail read it on the conference line. Your trainers know the scripts, she said. My nurses know the nights.
A. Swap cycle three for a pilot on one Wyoming unit the week of go-live.
B. Add UAT run by Wyoming's nurses and doctors, and trust the load.
C. Add a volume test at go-live load, UAT by Wyoming staff, and exit criteria.
D. Accept the plan, since the system carries eight hospitals every day already.

The plan comes back Monday with three changes. A volume test on Saturday, September 11, with scripts playing a Monday at seven in the morning: nine hundred users signing in at three hospitals, with orders, results, and transfers all flowing. UAT round one on August 17 and 18, run by Wyoming nurses, pharmacists, and doctors on their own scenarios, Walt included, and a short round two on the final build after build three. And exit criteria, written before anybody knows the score: 95 percent of scripts passed, no open severity one or two defects, every contract acceptance test passed, and a signature from each CNO. Gail reads the last line. Mine? Yours.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Each kind of test answers its own question. Volume testing finds where a system slows under real load. User acceptance testing lets the people who'll use it decide whether it's ready. Exit criteria, set in advance, keep anyone from deciding the bar after they've seen the score.

Wednesday, August 11, the Laramie surgeons' lounge, 7:00 AM. Walt had a clicker in one hand and a copy of the contract open to the acceptance tests. Corvane's trainer sat at the keyboard with a test patient, a routine gallbladder, ready to go home.
Walt clicked once for every click. He didn't say the number until the end. Forty-four.

Corvane's project director was on the phone from Denver. Forty-four is very close, and three of those are the pending results screen your own council asked for. We'd like to mark 7.3 passed with an exception and sign the build milestone Friday. We'll keep working the clicks after go-live.
A. Sign it with the exception, since it's close and safety added some clicks.
B. Fail 7.3, log the defect, and hold the milestone until it passes.
C. Accept it with a written exception, and a fix date after go-live.
D. Change the requirement to forty-four, since the signed design added steps.

Maria marks it failed in the test record, with Walt's count and the screen where each click happened. The milestone payment waits, as the contract says it does. Corvane's analyst sits with Walt that afternoon, clicker on the table. The pending results screen stays. Two acknowledgments become one signed list, an old diagnosis prompt goes, and the discharge order opens filled in. Friday at seven Walt clicks again. Thirty-nine. He puts the clicker in his pocket. Seven point three. Passed. Write it down.

Exactly right. Validate the build against the contract and the design specs, with the acceptance tests written from them. A failed test is logged as a defect, and the deliverable isn't accepted until it passes. The safety steps stay. The waste around them goes.

Thursday, August 12, the change advisory board met at two, eleven people around the table and Nate on the speaker. Item four was Corvane's. Before go-live, the Wyoming build had to be in Cascade's one Corvane production system, the same system the other eight hospitals used every hour of every day. Corvane asked for standing approval to move it every Thursday night: everything changed in test that week, hidden from the eight hospitals until October.
The request was two paragraphs long. Risk, low. Clinical impact, none.
Maria had read those words before, on a firewall change, ten months ago. So had Nate. None, he said over the speaker. That's a big word for a Thursday.
A. Approve each move with a listed manifest, impact check, and back-out plan.
B. Approve the weekly moves, if Corvane tests each package before it moves.
C. Hold all the Wyoming build out of production until the final week.
D. Approve it as a standard change, since the build stays hidden till go-live.

The board approves it with conditions. Every package lists each change by its ticket. Anything that touches shared content, like the order sets, alerts, and dose times all eleven hospitals use, gets its own ticket and its owner's signature. After each move, a short regression set runs at Greeley and Fort Collins. The back-out plan gets tested once, on purpose, before the first real move. Nate unmutes. Better.

That's the move. Technical change management asks what's changing, what it touches, what proves it's safe, and how to undo it. In a shared system, a change built for three hospitals can reach all eleven, so the impact check covers them all.

Tuesday, August 17, UAT round one came to Rawlins. Gail had put eight of her nurses on the schedule, nights and days, and paid them to be there. The fixed build passed script one in four minutes. All twenty-three medications arrived inside the admission reconciliation, each labeled with the sending hospital, as the contract said.

A night nurse with twenty-two years at Rawlins ran the next one: a test patient coming back from Greeley after surgery. She stopped on line nine. Warfarin, she said. Did they stop it for surgery, or is it still going? Where's the last dose?

The answer was on the screen, under a small gray icon, in text that appeared when you held the mouse over it. Corvane's trainer showed her. The nurse looked at him. At three in the morning, she said, I don't hover.
A. Pass the script, since every step finished and the data was on the screen.
B. Show each outside med's status and last dose time in its row.
C. Add a training tip about hovering on the icon, and pass the script.
D. Hide stopped outside meds from the list, so nobody can continue them.

Maria writes it up as a defect against the design, severity two, with the nurse's words in the description. Corvane moves status and last dose into the row itself: active, held, or stopped, with the date and time. Stopped medications stay on the list with a line through them. Pharmacy signs the change. On Wednesday the nurse runs it again and finds the warfarin, stopped two days before surgery, in under three seconds. Okay, she says. That's her yes, Gail says. Write it down before she changes her mind.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Functionality helps clinicians when the information for a decision sits where the decision is made, in plain view. Status and last dose time are what a nurse needs to continue or stop an outside medication. UAT is where you learn whether the screen does that for the people who'll use it.
Friday, August 20, Maria was brushing her teeth when the chat came in.

A message from Tasha Greene. Pattern. 23 tickets since 9 last night, from Greeley, Fort Collins, and two of the other Corvane hospitals. Most say the same thing. Evening meds showing overdue. BID times look wrong. None from Wyoming. None before last night. Last night was the Thursday build move. I don't think that's a coincidence.
Tasha had been right about every early warning she'd sent in a year, and she never sent a second message until somebody answered the first. Maria answered it with the toothbrush still in her mouth.
A. Back out the whole Thursday package, first thing this morning.
B. Have the desk work each ticket as it comes in, and watch for more.
C. Tell nurses to give evening BID doses at the old times for now.
D. Match the tickets to the move, undo the cause, then dig.

Tasha sorts them by the minute. The first came in at 9:12 PM, forty minutes after the move closed. Nineteen of the twenty-three say BID. Nate's team pulls the move's change log, and there it is: the shared frequency table, with BID's evening dose moved from five o'clock to nine for all eleven hospitals. It isn't on the manifest. An emergency change puts it back by 7:20. Pharmacy reviews every evening BID dose given late overnight, forty-one of them, mostly stool softeners and vitamins, and finds no harm, and Maria files it in the safety reporting system the same morning. Tasha sends one more line. Change log says Wednesday, 2:07 AM. Kiran's login. Tell him I'm sorry I'm the one who found it.

Exactly right. Help desk logs are early warning. Group tickets by time, place, and symptom, line them up against recent changes, and treat a cluster as one problem. Restore service first, with the narrowest safe back-out. Then find the root cause.

Kiran was in her office before she sent for him, gray in the face, with a printout. He'd made the change himself, early Wednesday morning. Cheyenne's nurses gave BID doses at nine in the morning and nine at night, and the Wyoming test patients kept failing on it. He'd meant to change Wyoming's schedule. He'd changed the table all eleven hospitals shared.
I tested it, he said. Two scripts. Both passed. I was going to file the ticket in the morning, and then the morning was a meeting about something else.
Corvane's migration tool moved everything changed in test since the last Thursday, ticket or not. The manifest the board had approved listed 211 changes. The tool had moved 212.
A. Take away Kiran's access to the shared tables until after go-live.
B. Have Kiran check every weekly package against the manifest himself.
C. Have a second analyst review Kiran's changes before each weekly move.
D. Move only ticketed, versioned changes someone else has tested.

By Tuesday the tool moves by ticket, not by date, and a nightly report compares what's in test with the approved list. Every build gets a version number, and every test result points to one. Nobody tests, approves, or moves their own change. Shared content needs its owner's sign-off: pharmacy for dose times, the council for order sets and alerts. Nate's team reads the audit log every Friday. Kiran reads the new rules. It was me. It was you, and a tool that let one person do four jobs at two in the morning. We're fixing the tool. Go home at five. He nods. He doesn't.

That's the move. Internal controls during testing keep what was tested and what gets promoted the same thing. Version every build. Move only approved, ticketed changes. Separate the duties, so a builder doesn't test, approve, or promote alone. Then review the audit logs.
Decision eight. Two in the morning.
Saturday, at 2:10 AM, her phone lit the bedroom ceiling.

A message from Kiran Bhatt. BID fixed the right way this time, on Wyoming's schedule, not the shared table. Reran all forty med scripts. All pass. Notes attached. You can tell Ochoa on Tuesday it's handled. Sorry again. It won't happen again.

She was in jeans before she'd decided anything. She was on College Avenue with the heater running before it hit her that she was doing exactly what he was doing, at exactly the same hour, for exactly the same reason. She kept driving anyway.
The analysts' room was dark except for his two monitors. He hadn't eaten. His hands weren't steady. He looked up at her and almost laughed. You drove in at two-forty to tell me not to come in at two.
Then he stopped laughing. Nobody called, he said. I just kept answering.

You told me in June you were the one they called at two in the morning, Maria said. I heard it. I told you to go home, and then I used every page you made after midnight. The transfer match. The forecast. That whiteboard. She sat down on the next desk. I think I taught you it was a compliment.
A. Take him home, route his fix through change control, train a backup.
B. Thank him, send him home, and let his fix move Thursday, since it passed.
C. Stay and help him finish the open defects, since go-live is close.
D. Write him up for Wednesday's unlogged change, so the rule sticks.

She drives him home herself and leaves his car in the garage. He's asleep before the second light. His fix waits for Monday, a ticket, and somebody else's test, though she can see it's probably right. She calls him Sunday at noon and tells him he's off with pay through Friday, and she doesn't let him argue. On Monday she writes down the skill, not a title: medication build, and the name of the second person who'll be able to do it. One of the junior analysts Marcus has been teaching starts building medications beside Kiran, then while he watches, then alone, with a sign-off for each skill. It costs Maria her best builder for a week, eight weeks from go-live, and she tells Ochoa so on Tuesday, in those words. At the top of Monday's page she writes KIRAN, as always. Under it, smaller, in her own hand: and me.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Staff competency can't rest on one person working all night. Define the skill, train a second person, watch them do it, and sign it off. Care for the person first. Then fix the role, so the system doesn't need a hero at two in the morning.
Monday, August 23, build two ran: 140 scripts, the first 120 plus twenty new ones at the edges. 126 passed. Fourteen failed. The exit criteria said 95 percent.

Tuesday at 7:30, Ochoa had an email from Corvane's project director on his desk before Maria sat down. To hold October 16, Corvane proposed that build three rerun only the fourteen failed scripts, not all 140. Full regression is a luxury at this stage, the email said. It was addressed to Ochoa, with Maria copied.

Ochoa read it. Then he picked up his cell, found Corvane's vice president in the contacts, and his thumb stayed over the name. Maria watched him. He set the phone face down on the table, slowly, the way you set down something hot.
I was about to call him and fix this for you, he said. Old habit. Thirty years of it. He slid the email across the table and turned his legal pad over. It's your project. Tell me what you decide.
A. Rerun only the fourteen failed scripts in build three, to hold the date.
B. Move go-live back a month, so every test can still run at full scope.
C. Keep full regression, defer two low-risk items, and add the vendor's testers.
D. Have the analysts test nights and weekends until build three passes.

Maria answers it in one page. Full regression stays. Two items come out of go-live through change control, each with its owner's agreement: video visits in the Wyoming portal, which nobody needs on day one, and a custom surgery report Laramie can pull from the warehouse until January. Corvane adds four testers for six weeks at its own cost, under the clause that ties its payments to acceptance. Go or no-go is set for Friday, October 8, against the criteria everyone signed in August. Ochoa reads the page, initials the bottom, and doesn't touch the phone again.

Exactly right. Scope, schedule, budget, and quality move together. When the date is at risk, defer scope through change control, add resources, or move the date, in the open, with the sponsor. Don't cut testing quietly. Quality is the constraint nobody sees until go-live.

Wednesday, August 25, with Kiran home for the week, Maria pulled up everything with his name on it. One Chart's medication build. The order set reviews for the council. The FHIR feed spec for Aisha's Meadowlark patch pilot, due September 15. The chart views for Bev's remote ICU pilot, due October 1. And the mapping for Penwright's discharge instructions, phase two, set to start the month after go-live.

Five projects. Each one had an owner who'd been told yes. Aisha's email came in while Maria was still counting. Hope Kiran's okay. Is the Meadowlark spec still on for the fifteenth? The cardiologists are excited.
A. Keep every date, and split Kiran's projects among the other analysts.
B. Pause everything but One Chart until go-live, so the team can focus.
C. Rank every project and its people through governance, and defer.
D. Bring in two contract analysts to cover his projects until go-live.

By Friday it's one page. Fourteen active projects, nine analysts, the team booked at 131 percent for September. The IT steering committee ranks them by strategy and risk, with Ochoa, Glenn's analyst, and Aisha in the room. One Chart comes first, and the fall security patches for the eight Corvane hospitals stay, because they can't wait. The Meadowlark spec moves to November 15, with the pilot still on for February. Phase two mapping moves a month. Bev's chart views stay, because they're small and her pilot needs them, and a junior analyst takes them. Kiran's five projects become two. Aisha writes back. Fine. November fifteenth, in writing. Maria calls Theo about phase two herself. It's the call she least wants to make. He hears her out. A month, he says. My boss will yell, and I'll tell him it's right, because it is. Then: Irene says you call her Sundays now. She told you? She tells everybody.

That's the move. Projects share the same people, so manage them as a portfolio. Put every project and its staffing on one page, rank them against strategy and risk through governance, and defer what can wait, each with a new date its owner knows.
Decision eleven. Seven in the morning.

Saturday, September 11, the volume test played a Monday morning that hadn't happened yet. Scripts signed in nine hundred users at Cheyenne, Laramie, and Rawlins, placed orders, scanned doses, printed labels, and sent transfers through Tributary, at the rate the census numbers said a real Monday would.

At 7:15 on the test clock, Rawlins slowed. Charts took nine seconds to open. Marcus had the network graphs up beside the queues. Every fifteen minutes, the Rawlins circuit jumped to 96 percent for about forty seconds, then dropped back.

Nate found it first. Your downtime computers, he said. Every one of them refreshes its copy in the same minute. And the imaging system pulls yesterday's studies right then too. They'd built the downtime view to protect Rawlins. At the top of every quarter hour, it was choking it.
A. Turn off the downtime view refresh at Rawlins until after go-live.
B. Order a bigger circuit for Rawlins, and rerun the test when it's in.
C. Accept the slowdown, since it lasts forty seconds four times an hour.
D. Stagger the refreshes, give clinical traffic priority, and rerun it.

Marcus spreads the refreshes across the fifteen minutes, one unit at a time. Nate's team sets quality of service on the Rawlins routers, so the chart and the Tributary feeds go first, ahead of imaging and the guest Wi-Fi. The imaging pull moves to two in the morning. They run the whole test again the next Saturday. Rawlins charts open in under two seconds, and the circuit tops out at 61 percent. Gail, on the video call from Rawlins, watches the graph flatten. So the fix was to stop doing everything at once, she says. Usually is.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Infrastructure has to carry clinical work at peak load. Test it under volume, find what competes for the network, and schedule and prioritize traffic so the clinical record goes first. Buy bandwidth when that isn't enough.

Tuesday, September 14, the Clinical Informatics Council looked at the last list before go-live. Corvane's build team had loaded every alert in Corvane's standard content into the Wyoming build: 412 of them. Cascade's own governed library, the one the council had spent the spring cleaning, had 231, each with an owner and a review date.
Aisha had the two lists side by side. A hundred and eighty-one alerts were on Corvane's list and not on hers.
Gail was on the speaker from Rawlins. My nurses have lived with MedaLink's six alerts for nine years, she said. How many do they get on October sixteenth?
A. Go live with Cascade's 231 governed alerts, and add more on request.
B. Use the governed 231, reviewed by Wyoming, and track every override.
C. Turn off every interruptive alert for the first month, to keep it calm.
D. Go live with all 412, and review the whole list after ninety days.

The council keeps Cascade's 231 and drops the rest. The three Wyoming chairs go through the 231 in two sessions and flag nine that don't fit, like a fall reassessment timed for a night tech Rawlins doesn't have. Those get Wyoming versions, each with an owner. Sepsis version two goes live with both tiers, the board column and the tight pop-up. One of Marcus's analysts builds a dashboard of override rates by alert, unit, and hospital, read every week for the first ninety days. Gail gets her answer: sixty-three alerts that interrupt, and a name to call about each one.

Exactly right. Decision support needs ongoing governance at every site: approved content with owners and review dates, a review by local clinicians for fit, and override monitoring from the first day, so the content keeps getting better.
Friday, September 17, build three finished at 4:40 in the afternoon.

One Chart test pass rate by build. Percent of scripts executed that passed. Build 1, August 2, 120 scripts. Build 2, August 23, 140 scripts. Build 3, September 13 to 17, all 140 scripts, full regression.

One hundred thirty-seven of 140. No open severity one or two defects. Three severity threes, each with a workaround on paper and a fix on the calendar. Every contract acceptance test passed, 7.3 included. UAT round two ran on that same build on September 20 and 21. Gail signed for Rawlins Tuesday afternoon, the Cheyenne and Laramie CNOs on Wednesday, and Walt, unasked, initialed the surgery page.

Kiran had come back on Monday, August 30, and gone home at five that day, and most days since. The analyst Marcus had been teaching had her first three medication sign-offs on the analysts' whiteboard, in Kiran's handwriting. On Wednesday the cafeteria cashier stopped Maria at the register. The young man was back, she said. Every day at 12:15. Then she looked at Maria's tray. You, too, lately.

Sunday, September 19, Lucia came home from Greeley for dinner with a bag of laundry and four weeks of nursing school in her voice. They'd practiced medication reconciliation in skills lab with plastic pill bottles, and her instructor made them read every bottle against the list out loud, twice. She says you count everything, Lucia said. Even when it looks finished. Maria passed the potatoes and didn't say anything at all.

On her way out to the car, Lucia stopped in the kitchen doorway. Twenty-seven days. Till what? October sixteenth. You said after go-live. She'd been counting. Of course she had. That's a date, Maria said. That's a date.
Saturday, September 25, Maria was on the back step with her first coffee when Gail called at 8:14. Gail never called on a weekend.

Our clinic across town opens for walk-ins at eight on Saturdays, she said. The front desk turned the computers on. Every screen in the building has the same note on it. Somebody wants money. The manager's reading it to Nate right now.
Maria was already reaching for her keys. It was three weeks to the day before go-live.
